Sub:-Traditional rights of tribals on forest lands-discontinuance of eviction 
of tribals thereof. 
Sir, 
All over the world, forestry, as a land-use, has survived on the concept of sustained yield 
which was ensured by creating compatible legal systems. In India, consolidation of forest laws 
started during the British period with the inception of Indian Forest Department in 1864 and 
scientific management of forests was introduced for planned and systematic management of 
the forests. The British Government enacted the first law on forests in 1865. To 
consolidate the law relating to forests, the transit of forest produce and other related matters, 
the Indian Forest Act was enacted in 1927. According to the Indian Forest Act, 1927, the 
Government can constitute any forest land or waste land which is the property of 
Government or over which the Government has proprietary rights, a reserved forest, by issuing a 
notification to this effect Commercial interests of the then British Government motivated it to 
declare more and more lands as reserved forests, without ascertaining the rights of the 
tribals and other forest dwellers. 
100 

[4 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
Even after independence in 1947, during the process of amalgamation of princely States, 
the activity of consolidation of Government forests continued. The State Govemment/UT 
Administrations proclaimed the lands of ex-princely States and the zamindari-lands as 
Reserved Forests. However, no effective steps were taken to simulaneously settle the rights 
of tribals and other forest dwellers. Absence of records of rights which never existed for 
these people, became the main constraint in resolving this issue. As a result, the rural people, 
especially tribals and forest dwellers who have been living in the forests since time immorial, 
have come to be erroneously looked upon as encroachers of forest lands. 
The burning human problem on non-recognition of tribal rights over land with its 
origin in faulty implementation of legal provisions in pre-independent India, and 
the same remaining unresovled even after independce, has, continued to attract 
public attention. Having acknowledged the gravity of the problem, the 
Government, has been contemplating ways and means to address it. Consequently, 
for the first time, the guidelines under the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 showed 
the way for legal solutions to the long pending unresolved problem of settlement of 
rights and the tribals and other forest dwellers living on the forest lands since time 
immemorial. Side by side, recognition of the concept of sustainable forest 
management through participatory approach, in the National Forest Policy, 1988, 
brought to the fore mutual interdependence of forests and people. Unlike the 1952 
Forests Policy which centred around production and commercial forestry, the 
Policy of 1988 gives due regard to the traditional rights of the tribal people on forest 
land. While recognizing the symbiotic relationship between the tribal people and 
forests, it also safeguards the customary rights and interests of the tribal people and 
forests dwellers on forest lands. 
To fulfil the commitments as enshrined in the National Forest Policy, 1988, in respect 
of settlement of people's rights, especially rights of tribals and forest dwellers, over forests 
lands in regulated manner, the Centra) Government on 18th September 1990 issued 
guidlines for settlement of disputed claims of tribals, which were reiterated on 30-10-2002, 
requesting State/UT Governments to consider the settlement of disputed claims of tribals 
over forest lands and to set up Commission/Committees at the district levels involving 
Revenue, Forests and Tribal Welfare Departments for the settlement of disputed claims of 
tribals and forest dwellers. The 
101 

RAJYA SABHA [4 March, 2005] 
State Governments/UT Administrations were also requested to submit proposals in this 
regard to enable the Central Government to take a final decision in the .matter in a time 
bound manner. However, the State/UT Governments could not implement the guidelines 
effectively and the issue remained unresolved. 
The situation of the tribals became more vulnerable when, in pursuance of the 
Hon'ble Supreme Court order dated 23-11-2001 in IA No. 703 in IA No. 502 in Writ 
Petition (C) No. 202 of 1995, the Central Government instructed all the State/UT 
Governments on 3rd May, 2002 to evict the ineligible encroachers and all post-1980 
encroachers from forests lands in a time bound manner. Consequent follow up action 
by the State/UT Governments for evicting the ineligible encroachers, brought more 
intensely to the forefront, the issue of the disputed claims and rights of the genuine 
tribals and forest dwellers. They could not be distinguished from encroachers, and 
were proceeded against. This generated much consternation. Various organizations 
took up the case of such tribals and forest dwellers whose disputed claims had not 
been enquired into, and who were being proceeded against and evicted. This prompted the 
Central Government to issue a clarification on 30-10-2002 to the effect that there is 
no change, in the policy of the Ministry with regard to regularisation of pre-1980 eligible 
encroachments, and the commitment with reference to forest-tribal interface on the 
disputed settlement claims remained valid. 
The Central Government in its continuous bid to settle the disputed claims of the 
tribals and the forest dwellers, and to legitimize their traditional rights over forest lands, of 
subsistence agriculture, and trade in MFP issued supplementary guidelines on 5-2-2004 
to encourage the State Governments/UT Administrations to take up the matter of 
settlement of rights of tribals and forest dwellers in the right earnest and perspective. 
However, before action could start on these guidelines, their operation was stayed by the 
Appex Court ex-parte on 23-2-2004. Central Government has moved an application before 
the Apex Court vacation of the order. 
After a critical examination of the issue of settlement of claims over forest lands 
and eviction of in-eligible encroachers of forest lands, what emerges is that the State/UT 
Governments were not able to distinguish between the encroachers, and the original 
tribals and other forest dwellers living on forest lands since time immemorial. 
The Central 
102 

[4 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
Government is convinced that the difficulty in distinguishing between genuine 
tribals/forest dwellers and in-eligible encroachers by the State Governments/UT 
Administrations is the main cause of the problems of tribals. Therefore, some kind of interim 
measures are necessary to safeguard the interests of the tribals and forest dwellers who have 
been living in forests since long, and whose disputed claims are yet to be settled. 
In view of the above, and without prejudice to Supreme Court's order dated 23-11 -2001 
and 23-2-2004, it has been found appropriate to request the State/UT Governments, that as an 
interim measures, they should not * resort to the eviction of tribal people and forests 
dwellers other than ineligible croachers, till the complete survey is done for the 
recognition of such people and their rights, after setting up of District Levei Committees 
involving a Deputy Collector, a Sub-Divisional Forest Officer, and a representative of 
Tribal Welfare Department, by the State/UT Governments as reiterated in guidelines dated 18-
09-1990 and 30-10-2002 of the Central Government. The State/UT Governments are advised to 
exclude such tribals/ forest dwellers, other than ineligible encroachers, from the eviction drives. 
Simultaneously, it is also clarified here that this interim measure does not stop the State/UT 
Governments from evicting the ineligible encroachers from forest lands. 
Suitable instructions may be issued to forest functionaries at all levels to keep the 
aforesaid in view while dealing with eviction of ineligible encroachments from 
forest lands.

Role of communities in conservations of biodiversity 
518. SHRIMATI N.P. DURGA: Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT AND 
FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) the role of the communities in the management and conservation of biodiversity 
under the Biodiversity Act; 
(b) what protection Government are providing on the rights of the community 
representatives; 
(c) whether any additional rules have been formulated for the Biodiversity Management 
Committees; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS 
(SHRI NAMO NARAIN MEENA): (a) As per Para 1 of Section 41 of the Biological 
Diversity Act, 2002, every local body shall constitute a Biodiversity Management 
Committee within its area for the purpose of promoting conservation, sustainable use and 
documentation of biological diversity including preservation of habitats, conservation of land 
races, folk varieties and cultivation, domesticated stocks and breeds of animals and micro 
organism and chronicling knowledge relating to biological diversity. 
(b) As per Section 14 of the Biological Diversity Rules, 2004, the National Biodiversity 
Authority shall consult local bodies before granting any permission for access to 
biological resources and associated knowledge to any user agency. The community 
representatives can exercise their wisdom and rights while consenting or disagreeing to 
any such request. 
(c) and (d) Rules under the Act have also been framed and duly notified. The same were 
placed on the Table of the Rajya Sabha on 23rd July, 2004 and on the Table of the Lok Sabha 
on 19th July, 2004. These rules also contained provisions relating to the Biodiversity 
Management Committee.

World Bank Report on Maternal Mortality Rate and AIDS 
532. SHRI R.P. GOENKA: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have reviewed a recent study of the World Bank on social 
progress and outlook highlighting inter-alia despite increase in public health expenditure the 
maternal mortality has worsened, going up from 424 per 1,00,000 in 1990s to540 per 
1,00,000 in 2000 and HIV infected has risen from 3.5 million in 1990s to 4 million in 
2000; 
(b) if so, the reaction of Government thereto; and 
(c) whether any fresh steps have been taken to upgrade the health facilities available 
to common citizens and strategy drawn up to effectively contain HIV virus already 
threatening large parts of the country? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) and (b) The National Family 
Health Survey-! (NFHS-i). 1991-92 estimated the Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR) for India at 
424 per 1,00,000 live births. The National ' Family Health Survey-ll in 1997-98 estimated the 
MMR as 540 per 1,00,000 live births. The World Bank Group in their publication 'Country 
Strategy for India-September, 2004' have mentioned that based on the existing data, the 
Maternal Mortality Rate has worsened. They have, however, qualified this statement to the 
effect that there are problems with the data for this 
117 

RAJYA SABHA [4 March, 2005] 
indicator in some of the largest States that raise questions regarding data at the national levei. 
The Report of National Family Health Survey-!! also acknowledges that the difference in 
the estimates of MMR of NFHS-I and NFHS-II is not statistically significant due to 
various reasons such as large sampling errors etc. The Sample Registration System (SRS) 
of the Registrar Genera! of India have estimated the MMR for the country as 407 per 1,00,000 
live births in 1998 which is the same period when NFHS-il have estimated the MMR as 
540 per 1,00,000 live births. It is thus not correct to say that the maternal mortality rate 
has worsened 
it is true that the estimated number of HIV infections in the country has risen from 3.5 
million infections in 1998 to 51 million infections in 2003. Reasons for rise in HIV 
positive persons are low awareness of people about HIV/AIDS in the country especially 
rural and female partners in the highly vulnerabie States; high proportion of migrant 
population; inadequate safe sex practices; and large number of vulnerable population. 
National AIDS Control Organization c onducted National Ba seline General 
Population behavioral surveillance survey in 2001. The finding revealed that 76% of the 
respondent have heard of HIV/AIDS and 46.8% of respondents were aware of two 
important methods of prevention and transmission, 11.8% of males and 2% of females 
reported sex with non-regular partner while 51.2% among males and 39.8% among 
females reported using condoms during the last sex with their non-regular sax partners. 
(c) In order to prevent and control the spread of HIV/AIDS in India, Government 
has launched a comprehensive National AIDS Control Programme, currently under 
implementation throughout the country as a Centrally sponsored scheme with following 
components:— 
- Preventive interventions for high-risk populations through targeted 
interventions adopting a multi-pronged strategy including peer 
counselling and behaviour change; 
  - Preventive interventions for the general population through programmes for 
blood safety, voluntary counselling and testing services, Prevention of Parent to 
Child, Transmission (PPTCT), Information Education and Communication 
(IEC); 
- Provision of low cost care and support services by providing 
118

community care services, treatment of opportunistic infections and 
prevention of occupational exposure; 
- Collaborative efforts to promote inter-sectoral programme activities 
including workplace Interventions and public private partnerships; 
- Build technical and managerial capacities for programme 
implementation through surveillance, training, monitoring and 
evaluation, technical resource gr oups, operational research and 
programme management. 
In order to accelerate decline of Maternal Mortality Rate, provision has been 
kept for upgrading Primary Health Centres for providing 24-hour delivery 
services, operationaiising the First Referral units for providing Emergency

Use of banned drugs 
537. SHRI ANAND KISHORE YADAV: Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that some common medicines that have been banned in many 
foreign countries are still allowed to be used in India; 
(b) if so, the number and details of such medicines; 
(c) the effect of using such banned medicines; and 
(d) the action taken/being taken by Government against such companies that are still 
producing these medicines? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE (SHRIMATI RANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) to (d) There is no system of 
global banning of drugs. Drugs withdrawn in some countries may continue to be used in 
other countries and the decision to ban a drug in a country rests on various factors such as 
disease pattern in a country, the varying reactions of certain ethnic groups in a given 
population to the drug, the availability of safer substitutes as well as the cost factor involved 
in the treatment of the disease. 
There is an adequate mechanism to review the status of the drugs in India as and when 
any serious adverse events are reported in international journals, WHO news letters or a drug 
formulation is reported to have been discontinued in some developed country. A National 
Pharmacovigilance Programme has been launched to capture data on advise reactions of 
drug use in the country.

Population explosion and food 
543. SHRI KRIPAL PARMAR: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that population of country has crossed one thousand 
million; 
(b) whether it is a fact that due to over population despite the efforts of Government, 
common man is not getting the basic facilities of food, cloth and shelter; and 
(c) if so, the efforts made by Government to check the increasing population and 
the results thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) and (c) It is admitted that growing population causes a strain on natural and 
civic resources of the country. 
Various steps have been taken to stabilize the population of the country. The National 
Population Policy (NPP) has been adopted by Government in 2000. The National 
Commission on Population (NCP) has been constituted under the Chairmanship of the 
Prime Minister to monitor the implementation of the National Commission on Population. 
The National Population Stabilisation Fund (NPSF), i.e. Janasankhya Sthirata Kosh 
(JSK) has been set up as an autonomous body with a corpus of Rs. 100 crore to promote 
peoples' involvement in Family Welfare Programme. An Empowered Action Group 
(EAG) has been constituted in the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare under the 
Chairmanship of the Union Minister of Health and Family Welfare to give focused 
attention to the 8 demographically weaker Slates. The Reproductive and Child Health 
(RCH) Programme was launched by Government in 1997 for provision of 
reproductive, maternal, child health and contraceptive services to the people. More recently, the 
Government has decided to launch a National Rural 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
142 

[4 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
Health Mission to provide comprehensive integrated primary health services throughout the 
country. 
The demographic indicators of the country have improved considerably. The Total 
Fertility Rate has declined from 6 in 1951 to 3.2 in 1999. The Infant Mortality Rate has 
declined from 146 in 1951 to 64 per thousand population. The Maternal Mortality Ratio 
has declined from 437 in 1992 to 407 per lakh live births. The decadal growth rate of 
population has declined from 24.66% (1981) to 21.34% (2001). Similarly, Annual Growth 
Rate of population has declined from 2.22% (1981) to 1.93% (2001).

Action plan on AIDS awareness 
545. SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) the outcome of the action plan that Government propose to bring about on 
AIDS to generate awareness and develop a multi-sectoral approach to check the 
spread of the disease; 
(b) whether it is a fact that Government have decided to include HIV/ AIDS as a 
subject in schools and colleges, and 
(c) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) An inter 
ministerial group has been set up headed by the Union Minister for Human Resource 
Development to formulate a multi-sectoral plan of action with various Ministries. The 
idea is to underline areas wherein HIV prevention education can be mainstreamed within 
the existing programmes of each Ministry. A working group has also been 
constituted, comprising representatives from the different Ministries. The 
Ministries are in the process of finalizing their sectoral plans. It is envisaged that the 
plans, once finalized by each department/Ministry, will be dovetailed into a multi-
sectoral plan. 
(b) and (c) HIV Prevention Education is already part of National Council of 
Educational Research and Training (NCERT) national curricular framework, and 
State units of State Council of Educational Research and Training (SCERT) are 
incorporating the issue at the State level in the text books as per regional 
requirements. 
The issue is also being transacted in a co-curricular approach, through the Population 
Education Package developed by NCERT for adolescents which has HIV prevention 
education featured prominently. In addition, NACO through its State AIDS Control 
Societies conducts the School AIDS Education Programme through its module 'Learning 
for Life' in a co-curricular manner. The module was designed in a consultative process by 
experts from NACO, NCERT, UNESCO and UNICEF. The focus is on age and 
culture appropriate information such that apart from raising awareness on HIV, it also 
helps young people develop life skills such as resisting peer 
144 

[4 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
pressure, decision making, etc. towards a safe and responsible lifestyle. The 
activities at the school level include, Training of Teachers and Peer Educators, 
a nodal teacher-peer educator approach among students, participatory activities 
like role plays, discussions, debates, competitions, question box and access to 
referral services, if necessary. 
Joint campaign for HIV and TB 
546. SHRIMATI S.G. INDIRA: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that India has the largest number of people with 
turberculosis; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that I ndia has also largest number of HIV 
positive people infected with Tuberculosis; 
(c) if so, the Government have any programme for joint campaigning for these 
deadly diseases; and 
(d) whether it is also a fact that  HIV patients are more prone to 
tuberculosis? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKS HMI): (a) Yes, India has the 
highest burden of TB cases in the world. 
It is estimated that out of 8.8 million TB cases occurring each year 
globally, 1.8 million occur in India. 
(b) India has an estimated number of 5.1 million HIV infected persons by 
2003. It is also estimated that 50-60 per cent of those infected with HIV have the 
chance of developing TB during their lifetime. 
(c) A Joint Action Plan is being implemented in 6 high prevalence States from 
2001-2002 and the same has been extended to additional 8 States from 2003-
2004. 
(d) Yes, Sir, HIV not only increases the susceptibility to infection with the 
tuberculosis but also increases the rate of progression from latent TB infection to 
active TB disease.

SHRIMATI PREMA CARIAPPA:

country as a Centrally sponsored 
155 

RAJYA SABHA [4 March, 2005] 
scheme with the following components:— 
• Preventive interventions for high-risk populations through targeted 
interventions adopting a multi-pronged strategy including peer

blood safety, voluntary counselling and testing services, Prevention of Parent 
to Child Transmission (PPTCT), Information Education and 
Communication (IEC). 
• Provision of low cost care and support services by providing 
community care services, treatment of opportunistic infections and 
prevention of occupational exposure. 
• Collaborative efforts to promote inter-sectoral programme activities 
including workplace interventions and public-private partnerships. 
• Build technical and managerial capacities for programme 
implementation through Surveillance, Training, Monitoring and 
Evaluation, Technical resource groups, operational research and 
programme management.

Programme as follows: 
• Parliamentary forum and State legislative forums established in 9 States 
to provide strong leadership at different levels of governance.

Hon'ble Prime Minister. 
• Mainstreaming HIV efforts in ongoing programmes of various ministries and 
departments.

• Proposal of expansion of ART services for six high prevalence States

[4 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
• Provision of services for management of HIV—TB co-infection in six high 
prevalence States has been started with support from Global fund. 
• Mass media campaign to achieve total awareness about prevention of HIV/AIDS. 
• Phase I human clinical trials of recombinant Adeno-associated Virus (AAV) vaccine 
started at National AIDS Research Institute, Pune from 7th February, 2005.

centres.

560. SHRIMATI KUM KUM RAI: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that spurious and sub-standard drugs are being sold 
dauntlessly in the country; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that the Department Related Parliamentary Standing 
Committee on Petroleum and Chemicals has expressed concern over sale of sub-standard 
drugs; 
(c) if so, the steps taken by Government to keep a check on 
manufacturing and sale of spurious and harmful sub-standard drugs; and 
(d) the action taken against the guilty persons? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) As per the feedback available 
from the State Drug Controllers, 38824,43138,40862 drug samples were tested during the 
period 2001 -2002,2002-2003 and 2003-2004, out of which 96,129 and 118 samples 
declared spurious and 3458, 3724 and 3499 samples declared sub-standard 
respectively. Therefore, 0.33 per cent, 0.29 per cent and 0.288 per cent of these 
samples reported spurious and 8.9 percent, 8.63 percent and 8.56 percent of samples 
reported sub-standard. 
Overall the aforesaid data revealed that around 0.3 per cent of drugs 
were declared spurious and around 8.5- 9 per cent drugs were declared as 
sub-standard. It may be relevant to mention that a drug may be declared 
sub-standard because of defects wh ich may not affect the therapeutic 
efficacy of the drug. , 
(b) Yes, Sir. 
(c) Manufacture of spurious/counterfeit/fake drugs is primarily a clandestine 
activity and trading in counterfeit products, including drugs, is reported world over. 
However, keeping in view the serious implications of spurious drugs on public health as well 
as the loss to genuine industry, the Government has taken the following measures to combat 
this menace:— 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
158 

[4 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(i) Detailed guidelines have been issued to the State Government to undertake focussed 
surveillance over possible movement of spurious drugs. 
(ii) A Capacity Building Project through World Bank assistance has been taken up to 
provide substantial assistance to State Government to upgrade drug testing facilities 
or to establish new drug testing laboratories. It is expected to increase the number of 
samples tested in the country from about 36,000 samples to 1,00,000 samples per 
year and to reduce the reporting time to less than a month as against the present period 
from 3 to 6 months. In addition, the project envisages extensive training of the Centra! 
and State/UT drug regulatory staff and the concerned personnel from the 
Pharmaceutical Industry and a campaign for Information, Education and 
Communication (IEC) for the consumers. 
(iii) Specific training programmes for reguiatory officials of State Government 
on logistics of intelligence work, prosecutions etc. has been conducted with the 
assistance of FDA, Maharashtra. This activity is proposed to be continued. 
(iv) In order to ensure efficient information exchange between drug regulatory 
officers in the country, in respect of licensing, sampling, prosecution, etc., a 
countrywide computer networking project has been undertaken by the Central 
Government This will enable the Central Government to regularly monitor the 
enforcement activities and recommend corrective measures. 
(v) Pharma industry and traders have been motivated to fight the menace of spurious drugs 
as a shared responsibility. A number of cases could be successfully detected 
through the initiative taken by pharma industry involving hiring of retired intelligence 
officers. 
(d) Under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, the responsibility for regulating the 
manufacture and sale of drugs including taking legal action against the unscrupulous 
persons rests with the State Governments. As per the feedback available from the State 
Drug Controllers, 538,449 and 570 prosecutions were launched and 171,105 and 166 cases

New Molecule on AIDS Treatment 
570. SHRIMATI N.P. DURGA: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the medical faculty and Scientist in the 
University of Geneva have developed a new molecule called PSC-RANTES which 
protects against HIV/AIDS virus; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the manner in which the new molecule would help in AIDS control? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) and (b) Yes Sir. 
PSC-RANTES is a synthetic protein. PSC-RANTES was created in a 
laboratory at the University of Geneva. There was a template: RANTES, a human 
protein that is produced in small quantities in our body. In the event of infection, 
RANTES stimulates white cells by binding to a receptor CCR5 on the cell 
membrane. In 1996 it was discovered that HIV also uses the CCR5 receptor to 
infect the cells involved in our immune system. In effect, CCR5 and RANTES race 
for the same receptor, when RANTES gets there first, HIV cannot infect the cell. 
However, despite this natural barrier, RANTES is not tough enough to fight 
off HIV infection altogether. So, in 1997 Prof. Robin Offord, Dr. Oliver 
Hartley and their team from the Department of Structural Biology and 
Bioinformatics in Geneva decided to tinker with the protein a structure in an 
attempt to make it more effective against infection. Seven years later, they 
achieved their goal by introducing chemical modification to only three amino 
acids in the original protein sequence. 
PSC-RANTES has the capability to block HIV infection. The idea is to use 
PSC-RANTES as a microbicide, in the from of a kind of cream. No conclusive 
clinical research has been carried out till now. Appropriate safety and efficacy 
studies are required. 
169 

RAJYA SABHA [4 March, 2005] 
(C) Topical microbicides that effectively block interactions between 
CCR5+immature Langerhans calls (LC) residing within genital epithelia and R5 human 
immunodeficiency virus (HIV) may decrease sexual transmission of HIV.

(b) Yes, Sir. Replacement of overaged signalling systems at 1494 stations

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS (SHRI R.VELU): 
(a) to (d) Repair and Rehabilitation of bridges is an on going process on Indian 
Railways. Railway undertakes repair, rehabilitation/ rebuilding of bridges on the basis of 
their physical condition as ascertained during annual inspections and not on the basis of age.

for rehabilitation are classified as Distressed Bridges. These, however, are neither unsafe

heavier axle loads and higher tractive effort. Based on such identification of bridges, allotment

Steel production 
607.      SHRI RAVI SHANKAR PRASAD: 
SHRI RAJ MOHINDER SINGH MAJITHA: 
Will the Minister of STEEL be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government have set a target to instal the 110 million 
tonnes capacity of steel production in the country by the year 2020; 
(b) if not, the facts thereof; 
(c) whether the assessment with regard to requirement of steel in the country by the 
said period has also been made; 
(d) if so, the assessment of the same; and 
(e) the additional capital investment required to invest the said production capacity? 
THE MINISTER OF STEEL (SHRI RAM VILAS PASWAN): (a) to (d) the steel 
sector was deregulated, delicenced and decontrolled in 1991-92. Thereafter, the market 
determines production targets and investment decisions in the steel sector. Nonetheless, 
it has been estimated that in order to become self reliant and globally competitive in the 
steel sector the country would require indigenous production of over 100 million tonnes steel 
per annum by 2020 from the 2004 level of 35 million tonnes. 
(e) In order to achieve the goal of over 100 million tonnes of steel production by 
2019-20, it is estimated that the industry would need fresh capital to the tune of Rs. 
230,000 crore. In addition funds would also be required for technological upgradation of 
the existing facilities.

and iron ore are so balanced as to serve the projected expansion in steel sector; and

environment the Government acts as a facilitator and operational decisions related to capacity 
expansion are taken at the plant level and depend upon market conditions. However, in the 
proposed National Steel Policy it has been estimated, that in order to become self reliant and 
globally competitive in the steel sector the country would require indigenous 
production of over 100 million tonnes of steel per annum by 2020 from the 2004 level of 
35 million tonnes. 
(b) Yes, Sir. 
(c) Does not arise in view of (b) above.

*103.   SHRI THANGA TAMIL SELVAN:† 
 PROF. SAIF-UD-DIN SOZ: 
Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that incidents of rape including minors is on the 
rise in the country; 
(b) the steps taken by Government to prevent this heinous crime; and 
(c) whether Government would consider imposing death penalty on rapist 
by amending the existing criminal law? 
THE MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRI SHIVRAJ V PATIL): (a) to 
(c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) As per statistics complied by the National Crimes Record Bureau, 
the number of incidents of rape reported in the years 2001,2002 and 2003 
were 16075,16373 and 15847 respectively. Out of these, the number of 
incidents of rape of minors during the same period were 2113,2532 and 
 †The question was actually asked on the floor of the house by Shri Thanga Tamil Selvan. 
16 

[9 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
2949 respectively. Total number of incidents of rape cases in 2004 (upto 
September-provisional) is 12414. 
(b) 'Public Order' and 'Police' are State subjects as per the Seventh 
Schedule to the constitution of India and, as such, registration, investigation, 
detection and prevention of crime is primarily the responsibility of the State 
Governments. However, the Government of India has been issuing advisories 
to the State Governments from time to time to make concerted efforts to 
improve the administration of Criminal Justice System and to take effective 
measures to control crimes against vulnerable sections including women 
and children. In an advisory sent to the State Governments in May, 2004, 
the following points have been re-emphasized: 
i. There should be no delay in registration of FIR in cases of Crime 
Against Women. 
ii. Cases should be thoroughly investigated and charge-sheets filed 
within three months from the date of occurrence of crime, 
iii. Women Police Cells be set up in all police stations. Exclusive 
women police stations may also be set up to cater especially to 
women, 
iv. Police officials charged with the responsibility of protecting women 
should be sensitized adequately, 
v. Women police officials in the State Police Force should be 
recruited widely, 
vi. Institutional support should be provided to victims of violence, 
and 
vii. There should be proper counseling to victims of rape. 
(c) The existing provisions of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, prescribe a 
sentence upto life imprisonment in case of offence of rape. The Law 
Commission and the Committee constituted for making recommendations 
for Criminal Justice System have not recommended death penalty for the 
offence of rape. There is no proposal under Government's consideration to 
introduce the sentence of death penalty for those guilty of rape.

the number of incidents of rape of minors has increased from 2113 in 2001 
to 2949 in 2003. These figures indi cate only the reported cases. Hon.

our social system, many cases of rape go unreported. So, I would like to

kind of sentence, that is, death sentence, will reduce the number of crimes

Additional Grants to Naxal Affected States 
 
*104. SHRIMATI HEMA MALINI: Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS 
be pleasd to state: 
(a) whether Union Government propose to float a plan providing additional 
grants to naxal hit States for road construction to contain insurgecy in the 
country; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the existing present grant allocated to backward districts affected 
by Naxalism? 
THE MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRI SHIVRAJ V. PATH): (a) to 
(c) A statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) to (c) The Backward District Initiative (BDI) component of the Rashtriya 
Sam Vikas Yojana (RSVY) also covers 55 naxal affected districts in 9 
States. This scheme provides an additionality of Rs. 15 crores as special 
Central assistance on 100% grant basis per year per district for a period of 
3 years so as to fill in critical gaps in social and physical infrastructure in 
these districts including for construction of roads. Road construction in 
naxal affected areas can also be taken up under the Pradhan Mantri Gram 
Sadak Yojana (PMGSY). However, there is no specific plan/proposal to 
provide funds to naxal affected States for road construction to deal with 
naxalism. 
SHRIMATI HEMA MALINI: I would like to know from the hon. Minister 
whether the Government intends to make a unified command for all the 
States and the Centre to fight this menace jointly. What are the rehabilitation 
plans made for surrendered naxalites? 
SHRI SHIVRAJ V. PATH: Sir, we have taken steps in consultation with 
the State Governments. Whatever the State Governments are suggesting 
and whatever can be accepted by the Union Government, we have accepted. 
We have not waited for the State Governments to make suggestions; we 
have ourselves given them help in many, many cases. What we are d is 
this. We are giving them paramilitary forces to deal with naxalite activities in 
the States. Up to this time, we were charging some money for the 
paramilitary forces supplied to them. We have taken a decision recently 
not to charge a single pie from the State Governments for this purpose. 
We are giving some funds to the State Governments to see that the areas,

understand that this has to be done through the State Governments and 
we are trying to do all that is necessary and possible for this.

*112. SHRI GIREESH KUMAR SANGHI: 
DR. T. SUBBARAMI REDDY: 
Will the Minister of NON-CONVENTIONAL ENERGY SOURCES be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether expanding at rate of over 30 percent per annum, the 
wind energy sector in India promises to emerge as an economically viable 
option to meet current power deficit of the country; 
(b) whether with 100's of wind turbines producing clean green energy at 
an economically competitive cost, t he/Indian wind energy market is 
emerging as the third most rapidly growing wind market in the world after 
German and Spain; and 
(c) if so, what are steps Government propose to take to improve wind 
energy further in the country to meet power shortage? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF NON-
CONVENTIONAL ENERGY SOURCES (SHRI VILAS MUTTEMWAR): (a) 
Grid interactive Wind Power installed capacity has progressively increased 
from about 250 MW in 2002-03 to about 500 MW in 2004-05 (April-
December, 2004) with an average annual growth rate of about 25%. A 
cumulative installed capacity of 2980 MW has been achieved as on 
31.12.2004 in the country. Wind powe r requires a set of incentives to 
remain competitive, including prefer ential tariff. Considering that the 
potential for setting up wind power projects exists only in 10 States, the 
intermittent nature of such power supply and its low capacity utilization 
factor, wind power is expected to play a supplemental role. However, the 
aim is that 5% of additional grid interactive power installed capacity would 
come from wind energy during the 10th and 11th plan periods. 
(b) The Country currently ranks at fifth position in the world after Germany, 
USA, Spain and Denmark in the wind power installed capacity. During the 
first two years of the Tenth Plan, 10% of the additional grid interactive 
power installed capacity has come from wind energy. 
(c) Wind power progress in the country till date is highly satisfactorily. 
Apart from preferential tariff in most potential States, few major components 
of wind electric turbine systems attract a concenssional rate of custom

THE MINISTER OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI KAMAL 
NATH): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The fall in prices of tea during the last few years, coupled with high 
costs of production, sluggish rate  of growth in domestic demand and 
increased age of tea bushes have adversely affected the viability of tea 
gardens, particularly the medium sized and financially weak, resulting in 
closure/abandonment of some tea gardens in the country. This has caused

(c) and (d) The Plantations Labour Act, 1951 provides for the welfare of 
plantation labour and regulates the co nditions of work in Plantations, 
including tea. This Act is administered by the State Governments, who are

restructuring/rephasing of irregular portion of outstanding term/working 
capital loans in the tea sector with repayment over 5 to 7 years with a

Statement 
Objectives, constitution and functions of national manufacturing 
competitiveness council 
OBJECTIVES 
The Main objective of NMCC is to provide a continuing forum for policy 
dialogue to energize and sustain the growth of manufacturing sectors which 
have potential for global competitiveness, current strengths and constraints 
of identified sectors, and recommend National level industry/sector specific 
policy initiatives as may be required for augmenting the growth of 
manufacturing sector. 
50 

[9 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
COMPOSITION 
Composition of the National Manufacturing Competitiveness Council 
consists of Chairman in the rank of Cabinet Minister. 24 Members to the 
Commission from various fields including senior Government functionaries, 
Professionals, representatives from Apex Industrial Organizations and 
various industrial sectors have been appointed vide Notification dated 
25th November, 2004, besides Member Secretary in the rank of Secretary 
to the Government of India. 
FUNCTIONS 
The National Manufacturing Competitiveness Council (NMCC) will advise 
the Government on industrial and sector specific initiatives that may be 
required for enhancing competitiveness of industries which would include 
sectoral and enterprise level init iatives, innovation and technology 
development (R&D), entrepreneurship promotion, infrastructure and enabling 
facilities, trade and fiscal policies and employment generation.

Purchase of Ship Chandlers for Indian Navy 
803. SHRI AMAR SINGH: 
SHRI ABU ASIM AZMI: 
Will the Minister of DEFENCE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that ship chandler purchases in the Indian Navy 
was made from middlemen instead of from the original equipment 
manufacturer at Visakhapatnam's Eastern Naval Command; 
71 

RAJYA SABHA [9 March, 2005] 
(b) if so, the details thereof and action taken against the officers 
concerned; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that Indian Navy incurred a loss of several 
lakhs of rupees on account of procurement of substandard equipments for 
air conditioning plant in the logistic department; and 
(d) if so, what action has been taken against the officials concerned? 
THE MINISTER OF DEFENCE (SHRI PRANAB MUKHERJEE): (a) to 
(d) It is a fact that during 1993—1995, the Naval Headquarters had authorized 
Material Organisation Visakhapatnam to procure spares through Indian 
trade (ship chandler purchase). 
A majority of the ships and submarines based at Visakhapatnam, 
acquired between 1967—1991, were of Soviet Union origin. With the 
disintegration of the Soviet Union (in August 1991), there was a breakdown 
in the supply of spares and components for these Soviet origin Naval 
Platforms. This was due to the non availability of information about the 
Original Equipment Manufacturers (OEM) in the erstwhile Soviet Union. 
Before the disintegration of the Soviet Union, the Navy's requirements 
of spares and components were being routed through two Soviet 
Government channelising agencies i.e., General Engineering Department 
(GED) and General Technical Department (GTD). The Indian Navy did not 
have a sufficient data base about the market prices of Soviet supplies, as 
before 1991 these were supplied on Friendship Prices', by GET/GTD. 
Allegations of malpractices against ship chandler purchase were received 
by Naval Headquarters. These allegations were examined by the Central 
Vigilance Commission (CVC) and also investigated by the CBI. However, 
no malafide in such purchases was established and the case was closed 
by the CBI. 
During November 1995 an Indian Naval Ship had reported failure of air 
conditioning equipment whilst at sea. A Board of Inquiry was thereafter 
convened to investigate the allegation of procurement of substandard AC

(SHRI SRIPRAKASH JAISWAL): (a) and (b) The National Human Rights 
Commission (NHRC) has issued comprehensive guidelines on the arrest

effective implementation. The guidelines provide, inter alia, that in case of 
arrest, the authorities concerned should exercise proper restraint and make 
the arrest only after being fully satisfied of the genuineness of their action,

the use of handcuffs or leg chains except as provided under the law, 
association of women police officers as far as practicable where the person 
or persons arrested are women, avoidance of arrest of women between 
sunset and sunrise etc. The guidelines also refer to the requirements to 
be followed for effecting arrests as laid down in the orders of the Supreme 
Court in the Joginder Kumar's case-(1994) 4SCC 260 and D.K. Basu's 
case (1997)1 SCC. 
The Government has also advised all the State Governments/Union 
Territories to follow all the requirements laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme 
Court in the case of D.K. Basu Vs. State of West Bengal whenever arrests

National Hydrogen Road Map 
867. SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO:  Will the Minister of NON-
CONVENTIONAL ENERGY SOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is true that Gove rnment are preparing a National 
Hydrogen Road Map and also thinking of launching a national mission 
on bio-diesel as a part of its efforts to encourage the use of alternative 
fuels; 
(b) whether it is also true that Government have also identified the 
Ministry of Rural Development as the nodal Ministry for this purpose; 
and 
(c) how the National Hydrogen Energy Board provide guidelines for 
making and implementing hydrogen energy? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF NON-
CONVENTIONAL ENERGY SOURCES (SHRI VILAS MUTTEMWAR): 
(a) Ministry of Non-Conventional Energy Sources have constituted a 
National Hydrogen Energy Board under which a Steering Group has 
been set up to prepare a National Hydrogen Road Map. The Planning 
Commission's Report—2003 on Development of Bio-fuel has 
recommended launching of a National Mission on Bio-diesel as part of 
the efforts to encourage use of alternative fuels. 
 128 

[9 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) The Ministry of Rural Development has been made the Nodal Ministry 
for processing the recommendations of the Report of the Planning 
Commission on Development of Bio-fuel. 
(c) National Hydrogen Energy Board consisting of Secretaries of various 
concerned Ministries, high level repr esentatives of industry and their 
associations, academia and other exper ts reviews different aspects of 
hydrogen energy including its production, storage, transportation, delivery 
and applications for transportation and power generation through a 
consultative process with the objective of providing guidelines in the 
preparation and implementation of the National Hydrogen Energy Road 
Map.

Wind energy for meeting power deficit 
869.   SHRI B.J. PANDA: 
SHRI KRIPAL PARMAR: 
Will the Minister of NON-CONVENTIONAL ENERGY SOURCES be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the wind energy sector in our country is 
emerging as an economically viable option to meet the current power 
deficit in different States; 
(b) whether renowned industrialists and other eminent personalities 
have been investing in this sector to exploit the potential; 
(c) whether the installed capacity in this sector is increasing at a fast 
pace and that the nation could be one of the biggest wind power producers 
in the world; and 
(d) if so, action-plan of the Government to harness the gains of this 
pollution-free source of energy? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF NON-
CONVENTIONAL ENERGY SOURCES (SHRI VILAS MUTTEMWAR): 
(a) A cumulative installed capacity of around 3000 MW. has been 
achieved as on 31.12.2004 in the country. Wind power requires a set of 
incentives to remain competit ive including preferential tariff. 
Considering that the potential for setting up wind power projects exists 
only in 10 States, the intermittent nature of such power supply and its 
low capacity utilization factor, wi nd power is expected to play a 
supplemental role. However, the aim is that 5% of additional grid interactive 
power installed capacity would come from wind energy during the 10th 
and 11th plan period. 
(b) Yes, Sir. 
(c) Yes, Sir. The installed capacity of wind power projects has increased 
from 242 MW in 2002-03 to 615 MW in 2003-04 and it is expected to 
increase in 2004-05. India presently ranks at the fifth position in the 
world in terms of wind power installed capacity. 
(d) Grid Interactive Wind Power Programme is essentially private sector 
driven. The steps taken by the Government to promote setting up of 
wind power projects include concessional import duty for wind electricity 
131 

RAJYA SABHA [9 March, 2005] 
generator sub-systems, excise duty exemption, ten years tax holiday on 
power projects, benefit of accelerated depreciation and loan from Indian 
Renewable Energy Development Agency (IREDA) and other financial 
institutions. Wind resource assessment studies are supported in various States 
for identifying new areas for deployment of wind power projects. Wind power is 
being given preferential tariffs in respective States. 
Private participation in power sector 
870. DR. MAM. RAMASWAMY: Will the Minister of POWER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) the steps taken by the Centra l Government to improve private 
participation in power sector; 
(b) whether there has been certain road-blocks which are hindering private 
participation in power sector; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; and 
(d) the steps taken by Central Government to remove these road-blocks? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI P.M. SAYEED): (a) The 
Electricity Act, 2003 which has come into effect from 10th June, 2003 
contains several measures to attrac t private investment in the power 
sector. Government has also initiated the process of reforms and re-
structuring of power sector which would improve the finances of the 
power utilities thereby attracting private investments. 
Under the Act, thermal generation has been fully delicensed and 
captive generation has been freely permitted, Central and State 
Regulatory Commissions have been set up and power trading has 
been recognized as an independent activity. 
Under the provisions of the Act, open access in transmission has 
been introduced to promote competition amongst the generating 
companies who can now sell to diferent distribution licensees across 
the country. Guidelines for competitive bidding for procurement of 
power by distribution licensees under the Electricity Act, 2003 have 
been issued.. 
The National Common Minimum Programme has reiterated the 
commitment of the Government to an increased role for private 
generation of power and more importan tly, in power distribution. From 
time to time, Government has taken serveral measures to increase 
private investment 
132 

[9 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
in the power sector. Also, 100% Foreign Direct Investment has been 
permitted in projects for elec tricity generation, transmission and 
distribution. 
(b) and (c) The major road-blocks which are hindering private participation in 
power sector are as follows: 
(i) Inability of SEBs and State Governments to provide an acceptable 
payment security. The revenues of the SEBs are not adequate, to ensure 
payments to Independent Power Producers. This is due to skewed tariffs and 
poor collection efficiencies. 
(ii) Delay in finalisation of various contracts such as PPA, Fuel Supply 
Agreement and Fuel Transportation Agreement acceptable to all the 
concerned parties. Protracted negotia tions on fuel prices, liquidated 
charges/damages, risk covering clauses etc. have caused delays in 
achieving financial closure in many cases. 
(iii) Court cases in the form of Public Interest Petitions etc. 
(iv) Withdrawal by equity holders and EPC contractors. 
(d) The initiatives taken by the Government as mentioned in reply to part (a), 
particularly regarding the reform and restructuring of power sector including SEB's, 
formulation of Central & State Regulatory Commissions, recognizing power 
trading as an independent activity etc. are expected to boost the confidence of the 
investors. Government has also been assisting to resolve issues coming in the 
way of the private sector power projects achieving financial closure. An Inter-
Institutional Group (IIG) comprising senior representatives from the financial 
institutions as well as from the Ministry of Power, has been instrumental in 
facilitiating financial closure of 11 private power projects having a total capacity of 
over 4000 MW in the last one year.

Tariff Structure in Power Sector 
888. SHRI SANJAY NIRUPAM: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased 
to state : 
(a) whether Government have revised the tariff in Power Sector; 
(b) whether the recovery of capital costs in the power tariff would be 
front loaded or back loaded; 
(c) the details about the tariff structure and its sudden impact upon the 
Power Sector; and 
(d) whether common people are the ultimate bearer for the above ? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI P.M. SAYEED):(a) to (d) Under 
the Electricity Act, 2003, the tariff for supply of power to various 
categories of consumers is to be determined by the State Electricity 
151 

RAJYA SABHA [9 March, 2005] 
Regulatory Commissions (SERCs) and in doing so these Commissions are 
required to be guided by the provisions contained in Section 61 of the Act 
which, inter alia, include the factors which would encourage competition, 
efficiency, economical use of the resources, safeguarding of consumer's 
interest and at the same time ensure recovery of the cost of electricity in a 
reasonable manner. The State Commissions are also required to ensure 
transparency while exercising its powers and discharging its functions. 
The SERCs shall also be guided by the principles and methodologies specified 
by the Central Commission for determination of the tariff applicable to generating 
companies and transmission licensees. 
In the terms and conditions of tariff for the peirod 1.4.2004 to 
31.03.2009, Central Electricity Regulatory Commission has provided that 
depreciation would be permitted applying straight line method spread over 
the life of the asset. In addition, advance against depreciation shall also allowed 
to meet debt services obligations by considering the repayment period of 
loan as 10 years. The fixed cost goes on reducing as the assets gets 
depreciated. 
Section 63 of the Electricity Act, 2003 provides that the Appropriate 
Commission shall adopt the tariff if such tariff has been determined through 
transparent process of bidding in accordance with the guidelines issued by the 
Central Government. 
Central Government has issued the guidelines for competitive bidding for 
determination of tariff for procurement of power by distribution licensees. These 
guidelines, inter-alia, provide flexibility to bidders by laying down that ratio of 
minimum and maximum capacity charge for any year shall not be less than 0.7 
to avoid excessive front loading or back loading during the period of contract.

PRASAD SINGH): (a) to (c) For supplementing the efforts of the States to

provides financial assistance to the States under a Centrally Sponsored 
Scheme namely Accelerated Rural Water Supply Programme (ARWSP).

based on 
• Rural population; 
• States under Desert Development Programme (DDP), Drought Prone

State; 
• Not Covered/Partially Covered villages; and 
• Quality affected villages.

allocated to Karnataka as per the laid down criteria and the entire amount 
has been released.

914. SHRI NAND KISHORE YADAV: Will the Minister of TEXTILES be

(a) whether Government have fixed any target for export of textile by

(c) whether it is also a fact that India has missed the opportunities of

(d) if so, the reasons therefor; and

THE MINISTER OF TEXTILES (SHRI SHANKERSINH VAGHELA): (a) 
and (b) The New Textile Policy (NTxP-2000) makes a vision statement to 
achieve textile and apparel exports of US$ 50 billion by 2010. However, 
the textile export targets are fixed on year to year basis, keeping in view 
the most recent export trends and potential for future growth in different 
textile sub-sectors. For the year 200 4-05, the textile export target has 
been fixed at US$ 15.2 billion. 
(c) and (d) India's textile exports to the major importing countries (United 
States, European Union, Canada) had been circumscribed by the annual 
quota limits placed by these countries under the erstwhile quota regime, 
which has had an adverse impact of flow of investments in India's textile 
sector. As the date for the final integr ation of quota restrictions started 
approaching, encouraged with the Government's initiatives, the industry 
has taken definitive steps by making consideralle investments to restructure 
the industry through modernisation and expansion of capacities. 
(e) Government has been taking a number of steps from time to time to 
strengthen the Indian textile indust ry to meet the emerging global 
competition. Some of the important initiatives taken are: 
(i) The Technology Upgradation Fund Scheme (TUFS) has been made 
operational from 1 -4-1999 to facilitate the modernisation and upgradation 
of the sector. 
181 

RAJYA SABHA [9 March, 2005] 
(ii) The imports of specified textiles and garment machinery items has 
been allowed at concessional rate of customs duty to encourage 
investments and to make our textile products competitive in the global 
market. The cost of machinery has also been reduced through fiscal policy 
measures. 
(iii) To improve the productivity and quality of cotton, Government has 
launched Technology Mission on Cotton (TMC). The mission comprises

State languages in school curriculum 
*82. SHRI SANJAY RAUT: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that some of the State Governments have made 
their State language compulsory in the primary and secondary level school 
curriculum; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) what would be the impact of su ch decision if other States also 
follow; 
(d) whether Government have taken any decision in the matter to make 
State language compulsory in primary and secondary level school's 
curriculum; and 
(e) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN R ESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRI 
ARJUN SINGH): (a) to (c) The Government is not aware whether any 
State Governments have made their respective State languages 
compulsory in the primary and secondary school curriculum. At the national 
level, the National Council of Educational Research and Training (NCERT) 
prepares the curriculum for school education. The Central Board of 
191 

RAJYA SABHA [9 March, 2005] 
Secondary Education (CBSE) adopts/adapts this curriculum for its affiliated 
schools only. The State Education Bo ards are not bound to follow the 
curriculum prepared by the NCERT. They are empowered to prepare their 
own curriculum for their respective schools. The subject "Education" being 
on the Concurrent List, information re lating to the actions by the State 
Governments about making State language compulsory in their respective 
curricula is not centrally available. However, as per Article 350A, it is the 
responsibility of the State and of every local authority within the State to 
provide adequate facilities for instruct ions in the mother-tongue at the 
primary stage. 
The Three Language Formula as advocated in the National Policy on 
Education was approved by the Parliament. The formula is applicable at 
the upper primary stage and has to continue upto the end of Secondary 
stage i.e. Class X. This formula provides for a study of the mother tongue 
or the regional language compulsorily as the first language. It also requires 
the study of Hindi, English and a modern Indian language, preferably one 
of the Southern languages in the Hindi speaking, Hindi and English in the 
non-Hindi speaking States. The National Curriculum Framework for School 
Education (NCFSE) 2000 of the NCERT has also included the provisions 
of the Three Language Formula. 
This formula, which flows from a policy decision, is to be reflected in 
the school curriculum. The role of the Central Government in the matter of 
the implementation of the formula is recommendatory. The implementation 
of the Three Language Formula is the sole responsibility of the State 
Governments. All the States/Union Territories had, accordingly, been urged 
by the Government from time to time to implement it. While all the schools 
affiliated to the Central Board of Secondary Education (CBSE) and the 
Council for the Indian School Certificate Examination (CISCE) have already 
implemented it, most of the States/UTs, too, are implementing this formula. 
(d) No, Sir. 
(e) Does not arise.

Closure of Private Universities 
*84.    SHRI MANOJ BHATTACHARYA:  
 SHRI AMAR SINGH: 
Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether about a hundred private universities in different parts of 
the country have been closed following  a recent judgement of the 
Supreme Court of India; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the steps proposed to be taken by Government to protect interest 
of a large number of affected students? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRI 
ARJUN SINGH): (a) and (b) The Supreme Court of India vide its 
judgment dated 11 February, 2005 in writ Petition (Civil) No. 19/2004: 
Prof. Yash Pal & Ors. Vs. State of Chhattisgarh & Ors., has declared 
the provisions of Section 5 and 6,  of the Chhattisgarh Niji Kshetra 
Vishwavidyalaya (SthapanaAur Viniyaman) Adhiniyam, 2002, to be 
ultra vires of the Constitution. All notifications issued by the State 
Government in the Gazette in the purported exercise of powers under 
Section 5 of the aforesaid Act, notifying the Universities, have been 
quashed and such Universities cease to exist. The Supreme Court also 
held that "the impugned Act which specifically makes a provision enabling 
a University to have an off-campus center outside the State is deary 
beyond the legislative competence of  the Chhattisgarh legislature." 
The Supreme Court also directed that if any institutions have been 
established by such Universities, steps may be taken for their affiliation to 
already existing State Universities. 
(c) In view of above, the Chhattisgarh Government has been 
requested to inform whether any specific intervention is required to be 
taken by the Government of India in the matter. The UGC has also 
been requested to examine the judgement and its implications, 
particularly for the bonafide students en rolled with these "universities' 
so that, should the need arise, the Commission could be requested to 
take appropriate steps in the matter.

Mushrooming of private educational institutions 
*89.    SHRIMATI SYEDAANWARA TAIMUR: 
PROF. M.M. AGARWAL: 
Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that lack of proper infrastructure in government 
schools all over the country has led to the mushrooming growth of private 
educational institutions; 
(b) if so, the steps being taken to improve the quality of education in 
government schools; 
(c) whether Government have taken any measures to check the very 
high fee structure (donations and building fund etc in the name of quality 
education; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN R ESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRI 
ARJUN SINGH): (a) It is not necessarily the case that the increase in the 
number of private educational institut ions is because of any real or 
perceived lack of proper infrastructure in Government schools. 
(b) Most Government schools are under the control of State 
Governments. The Government of India is responsible for schools run by 
the Kendriya Vidyalaya Sangathan, the Navodaya Vidyalaya Samiti and 
the Central Tibetan Schools Administration. It is Government's constant 
endeavour to provide a high quality of model school education. The Central 
Board of Secondary Education, to which all Central Government schools 
are affiliated, seeks to enforce a uniformly high quality of education. The 
National Council for Educational Research and Training is responsible for 
providing a high quality of textbooks and other material. 
(c) and (d) While in respect of private professional courses a central 
legislation has been drafted for vetting by concerned Ministries for circulation 
among States and other stake holders for comments, in respect of schools, 
the respective State Governments/UT Administrations are competent to 
take appropriate steps to prevent charging of donations to building fund or 
exorbitant fee.

Shortage of explosives in Coal India Limited 
611. SHRI R.P. GOENKA: Will the Mi nister of COAL be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is fact that the coal  mining operations of the country's 
largest coal producer and supplier, the Coal India Ltd., have been held up 
due to acute shortage of explosives; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefore and the extent to which production of 
coal has been affected recently; and 
(c) the details of short term/long term steps taken to ensure uninterrupted 
supply of the required explosives to the Coal India mines? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COAL (DR. DASARI 
NARAYANA RAO): (a) and (b) Due to shortage of explosives in the recent 
past both coal production and overburden removal have suffered in the 
mines of Coal India Ltd. While coal production has suffered more in the 
mines of Central Coalfields Ltd., Eastern Coalfields Ltd. And Bharat Coking 
Coal Ltd., impact of short supply of explosive has been less in other 
subsidiaries of Coal India Limited. However, overburden removal has suffered 
in many mines which will affect coal production in the coming months took. 
The main reason of short supply of explosives is inadequate availability 
of ammonium nitrate, which is the major ingredient of the explosives being 
used in coal mines. 
Due to shortage of explosives, total coal production in Coal India Ltd. 
has suffered to an extent of about 18 lakhs tones during the last three 
months. 
(c) The details of short term/long te rm steps taken for uninterrupted 
supply of explosives to Coal India mines are as under:— 
The Chairman-cum-Managing Director of Coal India Ltd. has conducted 
emergency meetings with the explosive suppliers to maintain regular supply 
as per Contract and have also taken up the matter with the main Fertilizer 
Companies in the country for augmenting the allocation of Ammonium 
Nitrate to the explosive-manufacturers. The matter has also been taken 
up by Ministry of Coal with the concerned Ministry for augmenting the 
allocation of Ammonium Nitrate to the explosive sector at the earliest.

nationalization there were 70 mine fire s in Jharia coalfield, which are

reserves of coal lost due to fire is estimated at around 37 million tonnes in

(d) The following steps have been taken to control/extinguish fire in coal 
mines: 
(i) Sand flushing into active fire zone from surface to under ground 
through boreholes. 
(ii) Surface blanketing to prevent breathing in of air to the fire area. 
(iii) Inert gas flushing from surface through boreholes to extinguish 
fire. 
(iv) Quenching of spot fire and mining out the quenched coal. 
(v) Sealing of the part of the mine under fire by construction of the fire 
stoppings/isolation stoppings. 
(vi) Application of fire resistant sealant in and around the isolation 
stoppings/fire stoppings. 
(vii) Regular monitoring with the help of Co-detectors, toximeter, air 
sampling and analysis of the same at colliery level. 
(viii) Trench cutting by mechanized means to excavate fire and to 
prevent spread of the same. 
(ix) Intentional flooding by water to quench the fire in some mines. 
Apart from above action, 16 schemes for dealing with fires and control 
of subsidence have been sanctioned and funded by the Government. Out 
of these, 8 schemes have been completed. A Master Plan has also been 
prepared to deal with fires and control of subsidence in Jharia coalfields as

619: SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH: W ill the Minister of COAL be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Coal India Limited (CIL) was making efforts 
by participating in global bids for allocation of coal blocks abroad and/or 
participating in the equity base of foreign companies as joint venture;

Coal Videsh Limited for this purpose; and

competition between two PSUs on such as issue was not desirable.

649. SHRI B.J. PANDA: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state:

mushrooming of private technical institutes in the country; 
(b) whether Government are aware that these private technical institute 
can create problems for the students co ming out of these institutes in 
getting job; and 
247 

RAJYA SABHA [9 March, 2005]

inorder to address grievances of the students of these institutes? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI M.A.A. FATMI): (a) to (c) The Government has 
permitted private initiative in technical edcuation since there is demand for 
technical manpower within the country as well as in the global market. 
The All India Council for Technical Education (AICTE) has been mandated 
to assure quality in technical education. The Council has laid down strict 
norms and standards for setting up new institutions of technical education 
and for introduction of new technical courses in existing institutions. The 
expansion in technical education is necessary, especially in the emerging 
areas of technology so as to keep pace with the global as well as national 
demand for technical manpower. The AICTE ensures that the quality of 
these institutions is constantly  monitored and upgraded so that the 
manpower produced by these colleges is accepted globally as well as 
nationally. For awareness of students, a list of approved technical institutes

AICTE also publishes notices, from time to time, in leading newspapers, 
cautioning all concerned to check t he approval status of technical

Reforms in existing education system 
†654. PROF. M.M. AGARWAL: W ill the Minister of HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have formulated a national programme to bring 
reforms in the existing education system, for providing excellent training 
to teachers and to ensure uniformity in the fields of education: 
(b) If so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the details of the amount sanctioned to various States under the 
Centrally Sponsored Schemes during the last three years? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI M.A.A. FATMI): (a) to (c) The education system 
in the country is guided by the Na tional Policy on Education, 1986 (as 
modified in 1992) which, among other things, envisages that effective 
measures will be taken in the dire ction of the common school system. 
The Policy also envisages overhauling of the system of teacher education 
in the country with emphasis on continuing education and the need for 
teachers to meet the thrusts envisaged in the policy. 
Educational Reforms are a continuous process. A Committee of the 
Central Advisory Board of Education has been constituted on 8.9.2004 
under the Chairmanship of Shri Tarun Gogoi, Chief Minister of Assam on 
the subject of 'Girls Education and the common school system'. The 
National Council for Teacher Education, a statutory body, is responsible 
for regulation and the proper observance of norms and standards in teacher 
education at the Elementary and Secondary levels. The revised Teacher 
Education Scheme for the Tenth Plan period envisages establishment of 
one District Institute of Education and Training (DIETV District Resource 
Centre (DRC) in every District and making them optimally functional and 
operational or improving the quality of programmes undertaken by them 
especially those of pre-service and in -service training so as to enable 
them to effectively play their nodal role in improving quality of Education, 
as measured in terms of levels of learner achievement. 
Three statements indicating the amounts released to various States/ 
UTs under Centrally Sponsored Schemes (Plan) during the years 
2001-02,2002-03 and 2003-04 are given in the Statement—I, II, III.

RAJYA SABHA [9 March, 2005] 
Illiteracy 
†655. PROF. MM. AGARWAL: Will the Minister of HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that as on date more than 36 crore persons are 
illiterate in the country; 
(b) whether Government have formulated any time-bound programme in 
this regard; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; and 
(d) the effective steps being taken by Government to increase the literacy 
rate as well as to educate the illiterate people? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI M.A.A. FATMI): (a) As per Census 2001, there 
were 30.41 crore non-literates in 7+age-group in the country. 
(b) to (d) In the Elementary Education Sector, Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan 
(SSA) has been launched with a holis tic and convergent approach, to 
implement Universalisation of Elementary Education in a mission mode 
with district focus. The goals of SSA are: 
• All children in School, Education Guarantee Centre, Alternate School, 
'Back-to-School' camp by 2003. 
• All children complete five years of primary schooling by 2007. 
• All children complete eight years of elementary schooling by 2010. 
• Focus on elementary education of satisfactory quality with emphasis 
on education for life. 
• Bridge all gender and social category gaps at primary stage by 
2007 and at elementary education level by 2010. 
• Universal retention by 2010. 
The National Literacy Mission (NLM) aims to provide functional literacy 
to non-literates in 15-35 age group. The target of NLM is to attain a 
sustainable threshold literacy rate of  75% of 2007. The thrust areas of 
NLM are improving female literacy in low female literacy areas, to organize 
residual illiteracy projects in areas,  which have substantial number of 
illiterates, and to set up continuing education centre s for providing 
opportunities for life long learning to the neo-literates.

†656. SHRIMATI KUM KUM RAI: Will the Minister of HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state; 
(a) the number of NGOs engaged to make Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan a

Fee Structure for IIM 
660. SHRI KALRAJ MISHRA. Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have thrashed out the question of fee structure 
for the Indian Institutes of Management, and the autonomy to be enjoyed 
by these Institutes and their managements; and 
(b) if so, the outcome thereof, indicating the policy laid down as a result 
thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI M.A.A. FATMI): (a) Yes, Sir. Indian Institutes of 
Management continue to enjoy functional autonomy. 
(b) The broad policy for the fee st ructure of Indian Institutes of 
Management is as follows: 
(i) All the IIMs will provide a need-based scholarship to both the first 
and second year students; 
(ii) All the students admitted, whose annual gross family income is 
Rs. 2.00 lakh and below, will be eligible for scholarships up to a 
full tuition fee waiver. 
The IIMs are empowered to take all decisions regarding fee structure.

available with the Ministry, for the year 2002-03, about 53 per cent students

(d) Some of the steps taken by the Government to reduce the dropout 
rate are: 
— Education has been made free for all children between 6 to 14 
years. 
— Monitoring of attendance by the community. 
— Micro planning and household survey to identify the dropouts and 
reasons therefor. 
— Organising retention drives. 
— Improving the quality of teaching to retain children in school. 
— Organising bridge courses/back to  school camps etc. to bring 
the dropouts back into school. 
— Providing cooked midday meal to boost the efforts towards 
"universalisation of primary education" by increasing enrolment, 
retention and attendance and simultaneously impacting on the 
nutrition of students in primary classes.

Statement 
Leakage of results of CAT Examinations 
As per the report received from the Indian Institute of Management, 
Ahmedabad (IIMA), CAT 2004 was conducted on November 21, 2004. 
Answer sheets were scanned by each of the institutes immediately after 
that. On December 1, the admissi on chairmen of all the IIMs and the 
Common Admission Test (CAT) center coordinators met at CAT Center to 
do all necessary checks for processing  of the results. The final CDs 
containing the scores and the confirmed complete addresses were sent 
to all the IIMs and to the scorecard-printing agency on December 15, 
2004. 
The CAT group decided internally that by midnight December 21/22, 
2004, the results would be displayed on the websites of all IIMs and that 
posting of the scorecards would also start simultaneously. This was an 
internal decision, and there was no public announcement about this date. 
Before displaying the scorecards on their respective websites, each 
284 

[9 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
institute goes through a process of te sting from the view point of easy 
accessibility prior to uploading on to the website. The testing for the IIMA 
website was done in the evening of December 20, and early morning of 
December 21, 2004. Since comprehensive process of testing requires 
uploading and testing on-line, it is possible that some candidates may 
have got access to the link by mere coincidence. As the whole operation 
is to be in the public domain in any case, such coincidences would be 
inconsequential in terms of the ultimate outcome. Moreover, only the 
individuals who furnish the respective Test Registration Number and Date 
of Birth can have access to their scorecard. 
The results are actually declared through the printed scorecard sent by 
registered post to every candidate who took the test and the printed 
scorecard is the only valid document showing the result. In the CAT 2004 
Bulletin issued in July 2004, it was clearly indicated that all eligible test 
takers would receive their scorecards by the end of December, 2004. 
However, to facilitate faster accessibility of results from the viewpoint of 
the candidates, CAT Group also decided to allow candidates to have access 
to the electronic version of their scorecards. This was done primarily with 
the objective of providing better service to the test takers. The exercise of 
prior testing was meant to ensure a smooth and trouble free access to 
everyone. 
As decided by the CAT Group, the results of CAT 2004 were placed on 
the website of each IIM by midnight of December 21/22, 2004.

Child Care, Housing, Shelter and Civic Amenities, Economic Empowerment, 
Legal Reforms & Law Enforcement, Rescue and Rehabilitation, Institutional

to take appropriate measures to implement National Plan of Action. Immoral 
Traffic (Prevention) Act 1956 is being made more stringent for traffickers, 
brothel keepers, pimps, clients to curb the demand and supply. The other 
activities include awareness campaign through TV. and Radio, sensitization 
of police and lower judiciary and involvement of NGOs in prevention and 
rescue activities.
